items.prompt: In a graph of a subway map, what does an edge stand for?
items.explanation: Nodes are the places; edges are the connections between pairs of them.

items.prompt: A friendship on a social app is mutual. Is that edge directed or undirected?
items.explanation: A mutual connection works both ways, so it is undirected.

items.prompt: A follows B on an app, but B does not follow A. Which kind of edge is this?
items.explanation: The edge goes from A to B only, so it is directed.

items.prompt: What does a weight on an edge hold?
choices: The name of the station it leaves from
A number like minutes or cost
items.explanation: A weight is the number attached to an edge: how long, how much, how far.

items.prompt: If every edge counts as exactly one step, the graph is called what?
items.explanation: With no numbers on the edges, every edge is the same one step.

items.prompt: How many nodes and edges does the 6-station map have?
items.explanation: There are 6 stations (nodes) and 6 tracks (edges). The 12 only shows up when an undirected list stores each track from both ends.

items.prompt: Which of these is a graph, with nodes and edges?
choices: A list of names with nothing linking them
A single number such as a total
People and the friendships between them
items.explanation: A graph needs both things and connections between them. A bare list has nodes only.

items.prompt: A one-way street between two junctions is best modelled as what?
items.explanation: Travel is allowed in one direction only, which is exactly a directed edge.

items.prompt: A team maps which service calls which. Service A calls B, and B never calls A. Which description fits that edge?
choices: Undirected: an edge always works in both directions
Directed: it goes from A to B only
Weighted: because every call costs some time
Cyclic: because A and B depend on each other
items.explanation: A call has a caller and a callee, so it is directed. Weighted would need a number attached, and a cycle needs a path that returns.
items.reference:
Nodes, edges and their properties
node: a thing (station, person, service)
edge: a connection between two nodes
directed or undirected: one way or both ways
weighted or unweighted: carries a number or not
Why: direction and weight are separate yes/no questions you can answer for any edge.
items.learnMore:
What a graph models

A graph strips a situation down to things and the connections between them. Once you decide what the nodes are and whether an edge works both ways, the same tools apply to maps, friendships and service calls.

Common mistake

Mixing up direction and weight. Whether an edge goes one way and whether it carries a number are two unrelated questions.
items.reflection: Think of something you deal with every day (people, tasks, places). What would the nodes be, and would the connections between them run one way or both?

items.prompt: A road map shows distances in kilometres and every road allows travel both ways. Which pair of properties describes the graph?
items.explanation: Two-way roads are undirected edges, and the kilometre figures are weights. The two questions are independent.

Undirected, because both users are part of the block
Weighted, because a block is a strong kind of relation
Undirected, because a pair can have at most one block
items.explanation: The relation is not symmetric, which is what directed means. Strength would need a weight; having two users involved does not make an edge mutual.

items.prompt: Fewest rides and fewest minutes picked different routes on the map. Why?
choices: One of them made an arithmetic mistake
The map has no shortest route
Both routes are the same length
They count different things along the path
items.explanation: One counts edges, the other adds up weights, so they can disagree.

items.prompt: Which algorithm finds the route with the fewest edges?
items.explanation: BFS explores layer by layer, so the first time it reaches a node uses the fewest edges.

items.prompt: Which algorithm finds the lowest total weight when no weight is negative?
items.explanation: Dijkstra always expands the cheapest known station, so it follows the weights.

items.prompt: On the example map, how many minutes does the fewest-rides route from Home to School take?
items.explanation: Home to Central is 6 and Central to School is 17, so 6 + 17 = 23.

items.prompt: On the example map, how many rides does the fewest-minutes route from Home to School use?
items.explanation: Home, Park, Mall, School is 3 rides and 4 + 5 + 6 = 15 minutes.

items.prompt: What does the word shortest need before it means anything?
choices: A definition of what you are counting
A bigger map with more stations drawn on it
A faster computer to run the search on
A graph whose edges are all directed
items.explanation: Shortest by rides, minutes or cost are different questions.

items.prompt: Using BFS when you really care about minutes tends to give what?
choices: A crash with an error message
A route that may be slower
items.explanation: BFS runs fine on a weighted graph; it just ignores the weights.

items.prompt: If every edge has weight 1, how do BFS and Dijkstra compare?
items.explanation: With equal weights, fewest edges is the same ranking as lowest total weight.

items.prompt: Two routes tie on rides but differ in minutes. Which algorithm is guaranteed to pick the cheaper one in minutes?
choices: Dijkstra, because it adds up each edge's weight
BFS, because it explores in layers and finds the closest first
Either one, because tied routes have the same length
Neither one, because no search can break a tie
items.explanation: BFS never reads weights, so which tied route it returns depends on queue order. Dijkstra compares totals.
items.reference:
Which shortest, which tool
fewest edges: BFS
lowest total weight, none negative: Dijkstra
home to school: 2 rides = 23 min, 3 rides = 15 min
BFS on weights: runs, but answers a different question
Why: name what you are minimising first; the tool follows from that.
items.learnMore:
Shortest is a family of questions

A path has a length in edges and, if the edges are weighted, a total weight. These are two different measures, and each has its own search algorithm. Choosing the right one is the first step, before any code.

Common mistake

Trusting the first answer a search returns. A route can be correct for the question the algorithm asked and wrong for the one you meant.
items.reflection: Think of a trip or task where the fewest steps and the least time are different. Which did you actually care about, and did you notice there was a choice?

items.prompt: A navigation app runs BFS on a road graph that carries travel times and reports the route with the fewest road segments. What follows?
choices: It minimises time, because fewer segments always means less time
It minimises segments, not time, so a faster route may exist
It is invalid, because BFS cannot run on weighted graphs
It is right, because shortest means the same thing everywhere
items.explanation: BFS answers a question about edge count. A long highway segment can beat several short slow streets in time.

items.prompt: How many cells does an adjacency matrix for 10 stations always have?
items.explanation: A 10 by 10 grid has 100 cells regardless of how many tracks exist.

items.prompt: What does an adjacency list store for each station?
items.explanation: Each station keeps just the stations it touches (and the weights).

items.prompt: Which layout holds a sparse network in less space?
items.explanation: The list grows with stations plus tracks. The matrix grows with the square of the stations.

items.prompt: In the matrix, what does a dash in row Home, column Mall mean?
choices: A track that costs zero minutes
No direct track from Home to Mall
Home and Mall are the same station
items.explanation: A dash marks a pair with no direct edge.

items.prompt: A sparse graph is one where what is true?
choices: Every pair of nodes is connected
There are no edges at all
Most pairs of nodes have no direct edge
All edges have the same weight
items.explanation: Sparse means few edges compared with the number of possible pairs.

items.prompt: For V stations, how many cells does a matrix always have?
items.explanation: One row and one column per station gives V times V cells.

items.prompt: How many entries does the list hold for the 6-station, 6-track undirected map?
items.explanation: 6 stations plus 12, because each undirected track is listed from both ends.

items.prompt: Which layout answers is there a track from A to B with one cell lookup?
items.explanation: In a matrix you read cell (A, B) directly.

items.prompt: A network has 1,000 stations and each has about 3 tracks. Which layout is smaller, and by roughly how much?
choices: The list, by a factor of about 3
The matrix, by a factor of a few hundred
They are about equal in size
The list, by a factor of a few hundred
items.explanation: The matrix has 1,000,000 cells. The list has about 1,000 + 3,000 = 4,000 entries, around 250 times fewer.
items.reference:
List versus matrix
list: V + E entries (V + 2E if undirected)
matrix: V x V cells, always
6 stations, 6 tracks: 18 entries vs 36 cells
200 stations, 4 tracks each: 1,000 vs 40,000
Why: real networks are sparse, so the list's size follows the tracks while the matrix's follows the square of the stations.
items.learnMore:
Choosing how to store a graph

The list stores only the edges that exist. The matrix reserves a cell for every possible pair, which makes edge lookups instant but wastes space on sparse graphs. Count the cells before choosing.

Common mistake

Choosing the matrix because it looks tidy. Its size is fixed by the node count, so a large sparse network pays for pairs that will never exist.
items.reflection: Think of a collection of things where most pairs have no relation (contacts, tasks, routes). Would you record every possible pair or only the ones that exist?

items.prompt: When would an adjacency matrix be the better choice?
choices: The graph is dense, or instant lookups matter most
Any graph with more than 100 nodes
The graph is sparse, since empty cells cost nothing
Never, because lists are always better
items.explanation: Its cost is fixed by the number of nodes, which is fine when most cells are filled or when one-cell lookups are the priority.

items.prompt: In what order does BFS visit stations?
items.explanation: All stations one edge away, then two edges away, and so on.

items.prompt: Which data structure gives BFS its layer-by-layer order?
items.explanation: First in, first out means older discoveries are explored first.

items.prompt: What is the visited set used for in BFS?
choices: To store the minutes of each track
To avoid entering a station twice
items.explanation: Marking stations visited stops BFS from re-entering one already reached.

items.prompt: BFS starts at Home on the example map. Which stations are in its first layer?
items.explanation: Home's direct neighbours are Central and Park.

items.prompt: How many rides does BFS find from Home to School on the example map?
items.explanation: Home, Central, School is 2 rides.

items.prompt: Does BFS look at the minutes on a track?
choices: Yes, it picks the smallest first
items.explanation: BFS has no notion of weight.

items.prompt: In a queue, which item is taken out first?
items.explanation: A queue is first in, first out.

items.prompt: What does BFS conclude when it empties the queue without reaching the goal?
choices: The goal is one ride away
The longest route is the answer
items.explanation: Everything reachable was explored and the goal was not among it.

items.prompt: During BFS from Home the queue holds School then Mall, in that order. Which station is taken next?
choices: Mall, because it is cheaper to reach
School, because it was added first
items.explanation: A queue is first in, first out. Cost and neighbour count play no part.
items.reference:
BFS on the subway map
layer 0: Home
layer 1: Central, Park
layer 2: School, Mall
layer 3: Library
Why: a queue plus a visited set explores by number of edges, so the first arrival is a fewest-edges route.
items.learnMore:
Layers, queue and visited set

BFS finishes every station at distance k edges before any at distance k + 1. That ordering comes from the queue. Marking stations visited as they are queued keeps it from doing the same work twice.

Common mistake

Expecting BFS to prefer cheaper tracks. It never reads weights, so among equal-length routes the result depends on the order neighbours are listed.
items.reflection: Think of spreading news through people you know. Who hears at each step, and why does the order they hear in follow the same layers?

items.prompt: BFS marks a station visited when it is added to the queue, not when it is taken out. Why?
choices: So the first track's minutes can be stored
So the queue stays sorted by weight
So the last layer can be skipped
So no station is queued twice
items.explanation: If marking waited until removal, two stations in the same layer could both add the same neighbour.

The 15-minute route has fewer rides, so BFS missed it

items.prompt: What does Dijkstra take out of its priority queue next?
choices: The station with the lowest total so far
The station with the fewest neighbours
The station nearest the goal on a flat map
items.explanation: It always expands the cheapest known station.

items.prompt: What does relaxing an edge mean?
choices: Deleting the edge from the graph once it is used
Replacing a cost when a cheaper route appears
Making the edge one-way from then on
Doubling the edge's weight each time
items.explanation: If going through the current station is cheaper, the neighbour's record is overwritten.

items.prompt: Which structure orders Dijkstra's candidates by cost?
items.explanation: A priority queue hands out the smallest total first.

items.prompt: On the example map, what total did Dijkstra first record for School?
items.explanation: Via Central first: 6 + 17 = 23.

items.prompt: On the example map, what is the final cost from Home to School?
items.explanation: Home, Park, Mall, School is 4 + 5 + 6 = 15.

items.prompt: Dijkstra needs the edge weights to be what?
items.explanation: Negative weights let a later route beat a cost already treated as final.

items.prompt: Which route gives the 15 minutes?
items.explanation: The other routes cost more, or use a track that does not exist.

items.prompt: On a graph where all weights are equal, what does Dijkstra give?
choices: A longer route than BFS finds
items.explanation: Equal weights make lowest total the same as fewest edges.

items.prompt: In the trace, Dijkstra records School = 23 first and later changes it to 15. Why?
choices: The first record was a mistake that BFS later had to correct
Central was taken before Mall, so the cheaper route through Mall was not known yet
The weights on the map change while the search runs
It averages the two routes it has seen
items.explanation: Central (6) is cheaper than Mall (9) so it was taken first, giving 23. When Mall was taken it offered 9 + 6 = 15.
items.reference:
Dijkstra's trace from Home
take Home (0): Central 6, Park 4
take Park (4): Mall 9
take Central (6): School 23
take Mall (9): School 15 (relaxed), Library 12
Why: expand the cheapest known station and overwrite any neighbour's cost you can beat; non-negative weights make a taken station final.
items.learnMore:
Relaxing edges

Dijkstra is BFS with the queue replaced by a priority queue. Because lengths differ, an early estimate can lose to a route that is found later, so it keeps correcting estimates until the station is taken.

Common mistake

Assuming the first cost recorded for a station is final. It is only final once that station is taken from the priority queue.
items.reflection: Think of a plan where your first estimate of the cost was later beaten by a route you hadn't considered. What told you the estimate was only provisional?

items.prompt: Tracks: A to B costs 2, A to C costs 5, C to B costs -4. What goes wrong for Dijkstra from A?
choices: It reports C at 5 and B at 2, which is the correct answer
It loops forever on the negative track
It finalises B at 2 and misses the cheaper 1 via C
It refuses to start because the graph is directed
items.explanation: B is taken at 2 before C. The route A, C, B costs 5 - 4 = 1, but B is already treated as final.

take Park (4): Mall 9

Why: expand the cheapest known station and overwrite any neighbour's cost you can beat; non-negative weights make a taken station final.

Relaxing edges

Dijkstra is BFS with the queue replaced by a priority queue. Because lengths differ, an early estimate can lose to a route that is found later, so it keeps correcting estimates until the station is taken.

Common mistake

Assuming the first cost recorded for a station is final. It is only final once that station is taken from the priority queue.
items.reflection: Think of a plan where your first estimate of the cost was later beaten by a route you hadn't considered. What told you the estimate was only provisional?

items.prompt: In a dependency graph, what is a cycle?
choices: A program that depends on nothing else
Two programs with the same name
A dependency chain that loops back
items.explanation: A cycle is a path that returns to its starting node.

items.prompt: In the three-colour walk, what does gray mean?
items.explanation: Gray nodes are the ancestors of the node currently being explored.

items.prompt: In the three-colour walk, what does white mean?
items.explanation: White nodes have not been touched by the walk.

items.prompt: In the three-colour walk, what does black mean?
items.explanation: Black nodes are finished, and nothing under them leads back.

items.prompt: Checkout needs inventory, inventory needs pricing, pricing needs checkout. What is this?
choices: A valid order starting with pricing
A cycle: no valid start order
items.explanation: Each one must start before another that must start before it.

items.prompt: Which search follows one dependency as far as it goes before trying the next?
items.explanation: Going deep before wide is what depth-first means.

items.prompt: Reaching a gray node during the walk means what?
choices: The path has looped back on itself
items.explanation: A gray node is still on the current path, so arriving there closes a loop.

items.prompt: A walk that touches each node and each edge once costs about what?
items.explanation: One step per node and per edge.

items.prompt: During the walk a node is reached that is already visited and black. What should the walk conclude?
choices: Nothing is wrong: it was fully explored with no loop
There is a loop, because it was visited before
There is a loop, because it has more than one parent
items.explanation: Black means finished with no way back to the current path. Two paths meeting is harmless.
items.reference:
Three colours
white: not looked at yet
gray: on the path being walked now
black: fully explored, no way back
gray reached again: a cycle
Why: only a gray node proves the path has come back on itself; reaching a black node just means two paths met.
items.learnMore:
Finding a loop with depth-first search

A plain visited flag cannot tell a loop from two paths meeting. Marking nodes gray while they are on the current path, and black when finished, separates the two. The order nodes turn black is also a valid start order when no loop exists.

Common mistake

Treating any repeated visit as a loop. In a diamond, the shared node is visited twice and nothing is wrong.
items.reflection: Think of a chain of promises or approvals in a group. How could you tell that one of them is waiting, through others, on itself?

items.prompt: app needs search and checkout; search needs pricing; checkout needs pricing. Why is there no cycle?
choices: Any node reached twice is harmless
Pricing is reached twice but never from itself; two paths just meet
The graph has too few nodes to loop
items.explanation: A cycle needs a path from a node back to itself. Here both paths end at pricing, which depends on nothing.

items.prompt: Implement `degree(edges, node)`. `edges` is a list of undirected tracks like `["A", "B"]`. Return how many tracks touch `node`.
items.explanation: A track touches the node if the node is at either end. Count those tracks.

items.prompt: Implement `hasEdge(edges, a, b)`. `edges` is a list of undirected tracks like `["A", "B"]`. Return true if a track connects `a` and `b` in either order.
items.explanation: Undirected means both orders count, so check the track against (a, b) and against (b, a).

items.prompt: Implement `neighbors(edges, node)`. `edges` is a list of undirected tracks. Return the names of the stations that share a track with `node`, sorted alphabetically.
items.explanation: Each track gives the node at its other end. Sorting makes the result predictable.

items.prompt: Implement `nodeCount(edges)`. `edges` is a list of tracks like `["A", "B"]`. Return how many distinct stations appear.
items.explanation: A set keeps each name once, so adding both ends of every track counts each station once.

items.prompt: Implement `totalWeight(edges)`. Each edge is `[from, to, minutes]`. Return the sum of all the minutes.
items.explanation: The weight is the third item of each edge. A path's total weight is the sum of its edges' weights.

items.prompt: Implement `outDegree(edges, node)`. `edges` is a list of directed edges `[from, to]`. Return how many edges start at `node`.
items.explanation: In a directed graph only the starting end counts, so edges that arrive at the node are ignored.

items.prompt: Implement `hasSelfLoop(edges)`. `edges` is a list of directed edges `[from, to]`. Return true if any node has an edge to itself.
items.explanation: A self-loop is the smallest possible cycle: an edge whose two ends are the same node.

items.prompt: Implement `isSink(edges, node)`. `edges` is a list of directed edges `[from, to]`. Return true if no edge starts at `node` (it depends on nothing).
items.explanation: A node with no outgoing edges can start first, because it waits for nothing.

items.prompt: Implement `canStartAll(deps)`. `deps` maps each program to the list of programs it needs running first, e.g. `{ app: ["db"], db: [] }`. Return true if there is a valid start order (no dependency cycle), otherwise false. A program may appear only as a dependency, not as a key.
items.explanation: Depth-first search marks a program open while it is on the current path and done when finished. Reaching an open program means the path has come back on itself, so no start order exists. A diamond reaches a done program, which is fine.
items.reference:
Write the walk yourself
BFS: queue + visited, closest first
DFS: open / done states, open reached = loop
set of seen nodes: each node entered once
undirected: do not mistake the edge you came along for a loop
Why: the idea is only yours once you can write the walk and see it handle a cycle.
items.learnMore:
Writing graph walks

Each walk needs a place to remember what it has seen, or it loops forever on a cycle. Decide first what counts as a new node and what counts as a way back, then the code follows.

Common mistake

Forgetting to remember seen nodes. The code works on trees and hangs on the first cycle.
items.reflection: Think of a task where you retrace the same ground. What would you write down to avoid revisiting it?

items.prompt: Implement `hopCount(edges, start, end)`. `edges` is a list of undirected tracks like `["A", "B"]`. Return the fewest tracks needed to travel from `start` to `end`, or -1 if there is no route. `hopCount(edges, x, x)` is 0.
items.explanation: Breadth-first search takes stations closest first, so the first time it reaches the goal is with the fewest tracks. The distance map doubles as the visited set.

items.prompt: Implement `reachableCount(deps, start)`. `deps` maps each program to the list of programs it needs, e.g. `{ app: ["db"], db: [] }`. Return how many distinct programs can be reached from `start` by following dependencies, counting `start` itself. The graph may contain cycles.
items.explanation: Exploring from start and remembering what has been seen counts each program once and stops on cycles, because a seen program is never entered again.

items.prompt: Implement `hasUndirectedCycle(edges)`. `edges` is a list of undirected tracks like `["A", "B"]`, with no repeated track. Return true if the stations contain a cycle (a route that returns to its start without reusing a track).
items.explanation: Each track merges two groups of connected stations. If both ends are already in the same group, the new track closes a loop. This avoids the parent-edge trap of colouring an undirected graph.
